title: The test at the hall of saints
hookLine: a woman arrives at a hall of saints with nothing but her hair, and the first thing she gets is a hard question
carry: anubhava: God known by experience, not rank
last: MY WANTING BINDS; THE LORD'S GRACE SETS FREE.

cards: A gathering of saints in the city of Kalyana, where people come to talk about God plainly, and to be tested. In walks a young woman who has left a king's house.

She has given up her clothes on the road; her long hair is all that covers her. Before she can sit, one of the saints, known for his searching questions, asks her something that would make anyone flinch.
Her answer is what the story keeps. Today: the walk from the palace, and the test at the door.

teach.b: Her tradition's story, in paraphrase. A local king, Kaushika, wants Mahadevi. The tellings differ on what happens next: some say she refuses him, some that she marries him on conditions he goes on to break.

Either way, she leaves. Her husband, she says, is the lord white as jasmine, and she has no use for one who dies and decays. She walks away from the palace, sheds her clothes, and goes on, covered by her hair.
She comes to Kalyana, where the Virashaiva saints gather around Basavanna in a hall the tradition calls the Anubhava Mantapa, the hall of experience. The name is the teaching.
Anubhava means experience: these saints, the sharanas, asked whether you had truly met Shiva, not what caste you were born to or whether you were a woman.

There Allama Prabhu, a teacher well-known in the stories for his hard questions, tests her. He asks, roughly: if you've truly given up the body's shame, why hide behind your hair? Her answer comes in more than one form.
In one, she says that until the fruit is ripe, the skin doesn't fall away. In another, that the covering is for the people looking, so the sight of her won't trouble them.
She doesn't claim to be finished; she says she's ripening. And she thinks of the people around her, not only her own freedom. The saints don't send her away.
Tradition says they welcome her, and call her Akka, elder sister. In the hall of experience, an honest not yet was enough.

how: Lingayat tradition tells Akka Mahadevi's arrival at Kalyana and her exchange with Allama Prabhu in its collections of the saints' dialogues, and her story is staged, sung and taught in Karnataka.

the hall of experience, open to all

games.q: you're Akka, standing before Allama in only your hair. he asks why you hide behind it, if you've given up shame. what do you say?
o: that you're finished, and have nothing to hide.
that until the fruit is ripe, the skin doesn't fall away.
games.why: in one telling she answers that she's still ripening; in another, that the covering spares the people looking. neither answer pretends.

practice: Bring to mind one place where you're not finished yet, a habit, a hurt, a hope, and without scolding it or pretending it's done, say quietly to yourself: still ripening.
Breathe in and let it be unfinished; breathe out and let it grow in its own time. If you pray, you can offer the unripe part to God as it is.

wordCard.voice: Akka Mahadevi. She left a king for the lord white as jasmine, came to Kalyana in only her hair, and answered Allama's test: until the fruit is ripe, the skin stays on.

orig.note: Kannada: the hall of experience, the gathering of saints at Kalyana in the Lingayat tradition.

carryVoice: Your line: anubhava, God known by experience, not rank. Akka didn't claim to be ripe, and the saints called her sister. That's today, done.
